documents.title: Sign in to Meridian
documents.context: Meridian is a business analytics workspace for teams that build dashboards, monitor data, and share reports. This guide explains the supported sign-in paths for a Meridian organization. Your organization address has the form company.meridian.example. Use that address before entering credentials because it selects the correct identity policy. Meridian never asks for a password by email or chat. An organization owner controls allowed sign-in methods. Contact your own administrator when a method is unavailable. Meridian Support can explain product behavior, but it cannot change an identity provider or disclose another user's access. Keep the browser open while you complete each sign-in check.
pages: Open your organization address and select Sign in. Enter the email address attached to your member profile. A password form appears when local sign-in is enabled. Use the Forgot password link if the password is unknown. The reset link remains valid for thirty minutes and works once. It becomes invalid after a successful reset or a newer request. Copy the complete link when an email client wraps it across lines. After five failed attempts, Meridian pauses local sign-in for fifteen minutes. The pause ends automatically and does not require a support request. A workspace invitation must be accepted before the first sign-in. Ask an owner to send a new invitation when the original invitation has expired.

Single sign-on organizations redirect members to the configured identity provider. Enter your work email first, then select Continue with SSO. Meridian uses the verified email returned by the provider to find the member. The values must match exactly, including the domain alias chosen by the administrator. A message that says the account is not assigned means the provider did not grant access to the Meridian application. An organization administrator must correct that assignment. A redirect loop usually means old provider cookies remain in the browser. Close all Meridian tabs, open a private window, and try the organization address again. Do not use the general sign-in page for an organization that requires SSO.

A verification challenge appears after local sign-in when multi-factor authentication is enabled. Enter the current six-digit code from the enrolled authenticator. Codes change every thirty seconds, so wait for a fresh code when only a few seconds remain. Set the device clock to automatic if every code fails. A saved recovery code can replace the authenticator once. Each recovery code is single use. Store remaining codes outside the device that runs the authenticator. An organization owner can require multi-factor authentication for all local accounts. Members receive a setup prompt at their next sign-in. SSO members complete the identity provider's challenge instead, because Meridian does not add a second challenge to that flow.

Sign out from the profile menu after using a shared computer. Signing out closes the current browser session but does not end sessions on other devices. Use Profile, Security, Sign out all sessions to revoke every active Meridian session. The revocation can take up to one minute to reach an open dashboard. Browser extensions that block storage can prevent a session from starting. Allow first-party cookies for the organization address and reload the page. Meridian supports the current and previous major versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari. Capture the displayed request reference before contacting support about a persistent sign-in failure. Send the reference, organization address, time, and browser name, but never send a password or recovery code.

documents.title: Passwords and multi-factor authentication
documents.context: This guide covers security settings for Meridian members who use local credentials. Organizations that require single sign-on manage passwords and authentication challenges in their own identity provider. Meridian stores no readable password and support staff cannot recover one. Security changes apply to the member across every Meridian organization that uses the same local profile. Use Profile and Security from the account menu to review these settings. Owners can require multi-factor authentication, but they cannot view member recovery codes. Treat every reset link, authenticator code, and recovery code as secret. Meridian Support will never request any of those values in a ticket.
pages: A local password must contain at least twelve characters. Meridian accepts spaces and common punctuation, so a memorable phrase can satisfy the rule. The service rejects passwords found in its breached-password list. It also rejects the member's email address as the password. Change a known password from Profile, Security, Password. Enter the current password once and the new password twice. A successful change revokes browser sessions other than the one making the change. API tokens continue to work until they expire or are revoked separately. If the current password is unknown, use Forgot password on the sign-in page. Repeated reset requests do not extend an older link; only the newest message can complete the reset.

Set up multi-factor authentication from Profile, Security, Authentication app. Scan the displayed square code with an application that supports time-based one-time passwords. Enter the first current code to confirm enrollment. Meridian then displays ten recovery codes. Download or print them before leaving the page because Meridian cannot display them again. Enrollment is incomplete until one authenticator code succeeds. If the page closes early, start the setup again and scan the new square code. A member can enroll one authenticator at a time. Add the Meridian entry to the new phone before you remove it from the old phone. Otherwise, keep a recovery code for the next sign-in.

If an authenticator code fails, first confirm that the code belongs to Meridian and the correct email profile. Then enable automatic date and time on the device. Meridian accepts the current time window and a small clock difference. A manually set clock can fall outside that range. Wait for a new code and enter it without spaces. A recovery code can complete sign-in when the enrolled device is unavailable. Enter the full recovery code in the recovery option, including its hyphen. The code is removed after one successful use. Generate a replacement set from Security after signing in. Generating a set invalidates every old recovery code, including codes stored in another location.

Remove multi-factor authentication only after confirming that the organization policy permits it. Select Disable under Authentication app, enter a current authenticator code, and confirm. Meridian invalidates all existing recovery codes at the same time. An owner policy can block this control. If the only enrolled device and all recovery codes are lost, follow your organization's verified account recovery process. Support cannot disable authentication from an unverified email request. Before contacting support, collect the organization address, member email, and time of the last successful sign-in. Do not include identity documents in the first message. Support will provide a secure upload route if the organization's recovery policy requires additional evidence.

documents.title: Billing and invoices
documents.context: Meridian bills each organization under the plan selected by an owner. Billing administrators and owners can open Settings, Billing. Other members cannot view prices, payment details, or invoices. A subscription uses one billing currency and one legal billing address. Changes apply to future documents unless the page states otherwise. Meridian creates an invoice for each completed billing period and for some immediate purchases. Taxes depend on the billing address and any accepted tax registration. This guide explains normal billing controls. It does not replace the contract for an Enterprise organization. Enterprise customers should compare the portal with their signed order form before requesting a change.
pages: The Billing overview shows the current plan, renewal date, billing interval, and charge estimate. Monthly subscriptions renew on the same calendar day when possible. A subscription that starts on the last day of a month renews on the last available day in shorter months. Annual subscriptions renew on the listed date each year. The estimate can change when seats are added or removed before renewal. Added seats create a prorated charge for the remaining period. Removed seats stay available until the next renewal and reduce the next invoice. Meridian displays a confirmation with the effective date before an administrator accepts a plan change. Save that confirmation with internal purchasing records when an approval process requires evidence.

Open Billing, Invoices to download a completed invoice as PDF. Each row shows the invoice number, issue date, status, total, and currency. Meridian does not alter a completed invoice after payment. Update the legal name or address before the next invoice when company details change. For a correction to a recent unpaid invoice, update the profile and contact support with the invoice number. A receipt is available after a card payment settles. Bank transfers use the paid invoice as the receipt. Invoice email recipients are managed separately from organization members. Add a shared finance mailbox under Billing contacts so staff changes do not interrupt delivery. Removing a contact affects future messages and does not revoke PDFs already downloaded.

Card payments can fail because of an expired card, an issuer decline, or a billing-address mismatch. Billing shows the last four digits and expiration month, never the full number. Select Update payment method to replace the card through Meridian's payment provider. A failed renewal enters a fourteen-day payment-retry period. Dashboards remain available during that period, but an owner sees a billing banner. Meridian retries the card on the schedule shown in Billing. Paying manually cancels remaining retries for that invoice. If payment remains unresolved when the period ends, the organization becomes read-only. Data is not immediately deleted. Update the method and pay the open invoice to restore normal access without creating another organization.

Tax fields appear under Billing details. Enter a legal name, address, and supported tax registration before the next invoice. Meridian validates the registration format but does not decide whether an organization is tax exempt. A validated registration can change tax treatment for future charges. It does not automatically credit tax from completed invoices. Download the invoice and provide its number when asking about an incorrect charge. Do not send card numbers or bank credentials. Include the organization address, invoice number, expected billing detail, and reason for the correction. Currency changes require a new subscription at renewal because completed transactions stay in their original currency. An Enterprise contract can define different invoice timing, contacts, or payment terms than the self-service portal.

documents.title: Plans, seats, and member roles
documents.context: A Meridian organization contains members, workspaces, and shared analytics content. Its plan sets product features and its purchased seat quantity sets the number of active members. Owners manage plans and membership from Settings. Billing administrators manage payment details but do not gain access to dashboards unless they also hold a member role. Role changes take effect immediately and appear in the audit history. Seat changes follow the billing rules shown before confirmation. This guide describes self-service plans. Enterprise contracts can reserve seats or define custom roles. When portal information differs from a signed order form, an owner should contact the contract contact listed in Billing.
pages: The Plans page compares the current subscription with available upgrades. Upgrading takes effect immediately after confirmation and can create a prorated charge. Downgrading takes effect at the next renewal so current features remain available through the paid period. Meridian checks active usage before accepting a downgrade. Remove features or content that exceed the target plan before retrying. A scheduled downgrade appears with its effective date and can be canceled until renewal. Annual and monthly billing options can have different unit prices. The confirmation shows the total, tax, renewal date, and billing interval. Review those values before accepting. A trial organization can select a paid plan before the trial ends. Unused trial time does not become account credit.

Each active member consumes one seat, including owners and billing administrators who also have workspace access. Pending invitations reserve a seat until they expire or are canceled. Suspended members do not consume a seat and cannot sign in. Deleting a member removes the profile from the organization but preserves authored dashboard history. Owners can purchase additional seats from Billing or reduce the quantity for the next renewal. Meridian prevents a reduction below active members plus pending invitations. Cancel unused invitations or suspend members before lowering the quantity. A seat added during a period becomes available immediately. The prorated amount covers only the remaining period. Seat counts update within a few seconds after membership changes.

Owners control organization settings, membership, billing access, and all workspaces. Administrators manage members and workspaces but cannot transfer ownership or close the organization. Editors build dashboards and data views in workspaces they can access. Viewers open and filter published content without changing its definition. Billing administrators can view invoices and payment settings. A member can hold a product role and the billing role together. Workspace permissions can narrow access below the organization role. Grant the lowest role needed for normal work. Before removing the final owner, transfer ownership to another active member. Meridian blocks an organization with no owner. Every role change records the actor, affected member, old role, new role, and time.

Invite members from Settings, Members by entering one or more email addresses and selecting a role. Invitations expire after seven days. An owner can resend an invitation, which invalidates the earlier link and starts a new seven-day period. The invited address becomes the member identity and cannot be edited after acceptance. Cancel the invitation and create another when the address is wrong. Domain restrictions can limit invitations to approved company domains. Guests outside those domains require an explicit owner exception when the plan supports guests. Export the member list as CSV for a periodic access review. The export includes role, status, last sign-in time, and workspace count, but does not include authentication secrets or dashboard activity.

documents.title: Usage quotas and limits
documents.context: Meridian applies quotas to protect shared service capacity and to match each subscription plan. A quota can limit stored rows, API requests, scheduled runs, exports, or members. Settings, Usage shows the current period, measured amount, and plan limit. Most counters update within five minutes. A warning does not mean data was deleted. It means new work can pause until usage falls or the period resets. Owners can change plans, reduce usage, or contact their account representative. Support cannot silently remove a plan limit. Use the metric name and displayed reset time when discussing a limit because different counters reset on different schedules.
pages: API requests use a rolling one-minute limit per organization. The Usage page shows the normal request rate and burst allowance. A response with status 429 means the current window has no remaining capacity. Read Retry-After and wait that many seconds before sending another request. Retrying immediately extends congestion and can delay recovery. Spread scheduled clients across the minute and use exponential backoff with random variation. Successful and failed authenticated requests both count because both use gateway capacity. Requests rejected before authentication do not count against the organization. The counter returns capacity continuously rather than resetting at a single clock minute. Larger plans provide higher rates. An approved temporary override, when available, appears on the Usage page with an expiration time.

Stored-row usage includes active imported rows and retained historical versions. Deleting a data source starts an asynchronous cleanup and the counter can take several minutes to fall. Archived dashboards do not reduce stored rows because their sources remain queryable. Open Usage, Storage details to see the largest sources. Remove unused imports or shorten a source retention period before starting another large load. Meridian rejects only the part of an import above the remaining allowance and reports the accepted row count. Correcting a failed import does not double-count rows that were never committed. A plan upgrade increases available storage as soon as payment succeeds. A downgrade is blocked until measured storage fits within the lower plan.

Scheduled-run quotas count each report or refresh when its execution begins. A retry started by Meridian after a transient service error does not consume another run. A user-started retry does. The monthly counter resets at 00:00 UTC on the first day of the organization's billing usage month shown in Settings. Paused schedules do not consume runs. When the quota is reached, queued schedules move to Paused by quota and remain visible. They do not run automatically after reset unless Resume after reset is enabled. Owners can resume selected schedules from the Usage page. Combine reports that use the same dataset when practical, and avoid minute-by-minute schedules for data that changes only daily.

Export limits cover the size of one export and the total number started during a day. A dashboard CSV export can contain up to two million rows. A PDF export can contain up to one hundred pages. The daily counter resets at 00:00 UTC. Canceling an export after processing starts still counts because capacity was reserved. A failed export caused by Meridian does not count after the failure is recorded. Narrow filters, select fewer fields, or divide a long date range to reduce file size. The Exports page shows retained files and their expiration dates. Downloading an existing file does not start another export or use the daily counter. Support needs the export reference and organization address to investigate an incorrect quota message.

documents.title: Export dashboards and data
documents.context: Meridian exports let members move a dashboard view into a file for review or sharing. The export uses the filters, time zone, and visible fields saved at the moment it starts. Later dashboard edits do not change a completed file. Access to the file follows the member's workspace permission at creation time. Export files remain available for seven days and then expire automatically. They are not a backup system. CSV is intended for data analysis, PDF for a fixed visual record, and PNG for one image. Before sharing a file, review its contents under your organization's own data handling policy.
pages: To export dashboard data, open the dashboard, set filters, and select Export, CSV. Choose the visible table or All dashboard data when the role permits it. Meridian creates UTF-8 CSV with a header row. Dates use ISO 8601 and the dashboard time zone. Null values appear as empty fields. Values containing commas or line breaks use standard double-quote escaping. Large jobs continue after the browser closes. Open Exports from the profile menu to check status. Ready means the download can begin. Failed entries include a reason and can be retried after correcting filters or permissions. One CSV can contain up to two million rows. Divide a longer period into separate exports when the estimate exceeds that limit.

A PDF export captures the visible dashboard layout at a fixed width. Select portrait or landscape and choose whether to include filter values. Wide tables may continue on later pages. Interactive controls, hover details, and animation are not included. Charts use the theme active when the export starts. Custom fonts can be replaced by a supported PDF font, which may change line wrapping. Preview the first pages before sending the file outside the organization. A PDF can contain up to one hundred pages. Reduce the date range or hide detailed tables if the page estimate is larger. The generated footer includes dashboard name, export time, and page number so recipients can identify when the snapshot was made.

Scheduled exports are configured from a published dashboard. Select Schedule, choose the file format, recipients, time zone, and delivery time. Email recipients receive a secure download link rather than an attachment. The link expires with the export after seven days. A recipient must sign in when the organization requires authenticated sharing. Schedule owners receive a failure notice when generation or delivery fails. Changes to dashboard filters do not update an existing schedule unless the schedule uses Saved dashboard state. Review schedules after a dashboard owner leaves the organization because ownership transfers do not always imply recipient approval. Pause a schedule before changing a sensitive dashboard. The next run uses the current dashboard definition and the schedule's saved filter values.

If an export remains Processing for more than fifteen minutes, refresh the Exports page once. Do not start many copies because each job reserves capacity. Check whether the dashboard itself loads with the same filters. A failed source query also prevents an export. A download that opens as an error page may have used an expired link; start a new export instead. Browser download controls can block the file without changing Meridian status, so allow downloads for the organization address. For support, provide the export reference, dashboard name, start time, format, and displayed failure reason. Do not attach a file containing customer data unless support supplies an approved secure upload location. Support can inspect job metadata without receiving the exported content.

documents.title: Schedule reports
documents.context: A Meridian report schedule runs a saved dashboard view at a selected time and delivers a link to the result. Schedules are useful for recurring operational reviews, but they must have a clear owner and approved recipients. The schedule time zone controls daylight-saving changes. Meridian records every run with its start time, outcome, and recipient count. Only editors and higher roles can create schedules. Workspace permissions still control which dashboard can be selected. Delivery does not expand a recipient's product access. Use authenticated links for sensitive content and review recipient lists as part of regular access checks.
pages: Create a schedule from the dashboard menu. Give it a name that states the audience and purpose. Select daily, weekly, or monthly frequency, then choose a local time and time zone. Weekly schedules can run on one or more weekdays. A monthly schedule set to day 31 runs on the final day of shorter months. Select CSV or PDF and save the exact filter values required for each run. Meridian shows the next three planned times before confirmation. Check them for daylight-saving changes and month boundaries. The first run occurs at the next listed time, not immediately. Use Run now after saving when a test delivery is needed. A manual run appears separately in history and consumes scheduled-run usage.

Recipients can be organization members, approved guest addresses, or a configured secure delivery endpoint. Enter one address per recipient and confirm the displayed domain. A distribution list is easier to maintain than many individual addresses when company policy permits it. Authenticated delivery sends a link that requires Meridian sign-in. Guest delivery sends a limited link tied to the recipient address and can be disabled by an owner. Never use an open link for dashboards with restricted business data. The schedule creator receives notices about rejected addresses and delivery failures. Adding a recipient affects the next run only. It does not grant access to files from earlier runs or make the recipient a workspace member.

Schedule history shows Queued, Running, Ready, Delivered, Failed, or Paused. Queued work waits for available export capacity. Running means source queries have started. Ready means the file exists but delivery can still be pending. Delivered means Meridian accepted delivery for every recipient; it does not prove that each email inbox displayed the message. Failed includes a reason such as source error, permission loss, quota, or rejected endpoint. Paused schedules keep their configuration but create no runs. A schedule pauses automatically after five consecutive failures to prevent repeated noise. Correct the cause, use Run now once, then resume recurring delivery after the manual run succeeds. Keep the successful run reference when asking support about a recurring difference.

A schedule belongs to one active member. When that member is suspended or removed, Meridian pauses the schedule and alerts organization owners. An owner can transfer it to another editor from Settings, Schedules. Transfer does not change recipients, saved filters, or time zone. Review all three before resuming. Dashboard deletion permanently disables related schedules. Dashboard renaming updates the visible name but not a schedule's purpose text. Export files expire after seven days even when created by a recurring schedule. Download important reports into an approved record system when retention is required. Delete schedules that no longer serve an audience. A paused schedule still appears in access reviews because its recipient list remains configured and could be resumed later.

documents.title: Authenticate to the Meridian API
documents.context: The Meridian API lets approved clients read analytics metadata, start exports, and manage selected resources. Every request uses HTTPS and an access token. Tokens represent a service account or member and cannot exceed that identity's organization permissions. Create separate tokens for separate clients so one can be revoked without interrupting others. Never put a token in a URL, source repository, support ticket, or browser log. Meridian displays a token value once at creation. Store it in a managed secret store. API access uses the organization address and versioned path documented for the endpoint.
pages: Create a service token from Settings, Developer, Tokens when the plan and role allow it. Enter a descriptive name, select the minimum scopes, and set an expiration date. Meridian shows the new value once. Copy it directly into the client's secret store and close the dialog. Token prefixes identify the token record but are not credentials. The list later shows name, prefix, scopes, creator, last use, and expiration. It never shows the secret again. If the value is lost, revoke the token and create another. Do not share one token across development, test, and production. Separate values make audit history clear and allow safe rotation. Organization owners can review and revoke every token, including tokens created by a former member.

Send the token in the Authorization header using the Bearer scheme. A valid header has the form Authorization: Bearer followed by one space and the complete token. Do not use a query parameter. Set Content-Type to application/json for JSON request bodies and Accept to application/json for responses. Use the organization API host shown in Developer settings because a general host can select the wrong tenant. The API returns a request identifier in each response. Record that identifier with status, endpoint, and time. Never record the Authorization header. A 401 response means the token is absent, malformed, expired, or revoked. A 403 response means the authenticated identity lacks the required scope or resource permission.

Rotate a token before its expiration date. Create the replacement with the same or narrower scopes, update the client secret, and send a harmless verification request. Confirm the new token's last-use time in Developer settings. Then revoke the old token. Running both briefly avoids downtime, but keep the overlap short and documented. Revocation takes effect within one minute across API gateways. A request already accepted can finish. If a token may have been exposed, revoke it first and investigate client failures afterward. Search client logs by token prefix, not secret value. Changing a member password does not revoke service tokens. Removing the creating member also does not revoke an organization-owned service token, so owners must include tokens in offboarding reviews.

Clients should use a connection timeout and an overall request timeout. Retry only safe operations or requests that carry the endpoint's idempotency key. Honor Retry-After for rate limits and temporary service responses. Use exponential backoff with random variation and a fixed maximum attempt count. A response body can contain a structured error code, message, field details, and request identifier. Branch on the code instead of matching message text, because messages can become clearer without changing behavior. Pin the API version in the request path and review its deprecation date. Meridian announces version retirement in Developer settings and email. Test a new version with a separate client before changing production. Keep tokens outside configuration files that can enter version control.

documents.title: Meridian API error codes
documents.context: Meridian API errors use an HTTP status and a stable JSON code. The body also contains a human message, request identifier, and optional field details. Client logic should use the status and code. Message wording can change. Save the request identifier when diagnosing a failure because support uses it to find gateway and service records. Error bodies never require a client to send its token back to support. A single operation can fail before it reaches the target service, so the same status can have different codes. Handle documented codes and use a safe general branch for unknown codes.
pages: Authentication failures return 401. The code auth_missing means the Authorization header was not sent. auth_scheme_invalid means the header did not use the Bearer scheme. token_invalid means the value cannot identify an active token. token_expired means its expiration time has passed, and token_revoked means an owner revoked it. Correct the credential before retrying. Repeated retries with the same value cannot succeed. Permission failures return 403 after authentication. scope_required names a missing token scope. resource_forbidden means the identity cannot access the requested workspace or object. plan_restricted means the endpoint is not included in the organization's plan. Ask an owner to change access or plan settings. A broader token label cannot exceed the creator's actual permissions.

Request validation failures return 400 or 422. json_invalid means the body is not valid JSON. field_required identifies an omitted required field. field_invalid identifies a value with the wrong type, range, or format. filter_invalid means the filter expression cannot be parsed. pagination_invalid means the cursor and page controls conflict. Correct the request before retrying. A 404 with resource_not_found means no visible resource matches the identifier. Meridian uses the same response when an object exists outside the caller's permissions, which avoids disclosing its existence. version_not_found means the API version in the path is unsupported. endpoint_not_found means the method and path pair is not documented. Compare the request with the selected API version rather than guessing another path.

Conflict responses return 409. name_conflict means a resource with the same unique name already exists. version_conflict means the supplied revision is older than the current resource. idempotency_conflict means one idempotency key was reused with different request content. Fetch the current resource before deciding whether to retry a version conflict. Capacity responses use 413 for payload_too_large and 429 for rate_limited. A rate-limited response includes Retry-After in seconds. Wait for that duration and reduce concurrency. Do not retry an oversized body without changing it. quota_exceeded can appear as 422 when an operation would exceed a plan quota. This quota does not reset in the current request window. Review Usage or reduce the proposed operation.

Service failures use 500, 502, 503, or 504. internal_error means Meridian could not complete valid work. dependency_unavailable means a required internal component is temporarily unavailable. service_unavailable means the endpoint is not accepting work, often during a short incident. deadline_exceeded means processing passed the service time limit. Retry safe requests with exponential backoff and a maximum attempt count. Preserve an idempotency key when retrying a supported write. Do not retry validation, authentication, permission, or conflict errors without correcting their cause. Check Meridian status when failures affect several endpoints or organizations. For support, provide the request identifier, UTC time, method, path without private query values, status, code, and retry result. Remove authorization headers and sensitive request fields from every example.

documents.title: Webhooks and integrations
documents.context: Meridian webhooks notify an HTTPS endpoint after selected organization events. A webhook is a delivery mechanism, not a permanent event archive. The receiving service must verify each signature, respond quickly, and process repeat deliveries safely. Owners configure endpoints from Settings, Developer, Webhooks. Each endpoint has its own signing secret and event selection. Meridian displays the secret once. Store it with the receiving service and rotate it when ownership changes or exposure is suspected. Delivery history retains metadata and response excerpts for seven days. It can help diagnosis but must not contain credentials returned by the endpoint.
pages: Create an endpoint by entering an HTTPS URL, description, and event types. Meridian sends a verification delivery before enabling it. The endpoint must accept POST and return a 2xx status within five seconds. Redirects are not followed. Private network addresses, URLs with embedded credentials, and unsupported ports are rejected. After verification, copy the signing secret into the receiver's secret store. Do not put it in source code. Use separate endpoints and secrets for development and production. Event selection can be changed later without replacing the secret. Disabling an endpoint stops new deliveries but retains its configuration and recent history. Deleting it removes the secret and cannot be undone. Create a replacement before deleting an endpoint used by active automation.

Each request contains an event identifier, event type, creation time, organization identifier, and data object. The signature header covers the exact request bytes and timestamp. Verify that the timestamp is within five minutes. Compute the documented keyed digest with the endpoint secret. Compare it in constant time. Parse JSON only after signature verification. Reject a bad signature with 401. Return 2xx after accepting a verified event into a durable queue. Do not wait for slow business processing before responding. Event identifiers remain stable across retries, so store processed identifiers and make handlers idempotent. Event order is usually chronological but is not guaranteed across separate resources. Use the resource revision or fetch current state when order affects correctness.

Meridian retries a delivery after a timeout or non-2xx response. Delays increase across attempts for up to twenty-four hours. The same event identifier and payload are used, but each attempt has a new delivery identifier and signature timestamp. A 410 response disables the endpoint immediately because it means the receiver is intentionally gone. A 429 response follows Retry-After when it is within the remaining retry window. Other 4xx responses are retried less often than 5xx responses. Delivery history shows attempt time, status, duration, and a shortened response body. Keep endpoint responses small and free of secrets. Use Replay from history for a manual test. A replay is another delivery of the original event and must be safe to process again.

Rotate a signing secret from the endpoint menu. Meridian displays a new secret and keeps the old secret valid for one hour. Update the receiver during that overlap and verify a test delivery before the old value expires. A receiver can temporarily accept signatures from both secrets. Remove the old value after a successful test. For persistent failures, confirm public DNS, certificate validity, supported TLS, firewall rules, response time, and signature handling. Compare the delivery identifier and UTC attempt time with receiver logs. Contact support with the organization address, endpoint identifier, event type, delivery identifier, status, and time. Do not send the signing secret or full payload. Support can inspect delivery metadata without receiving customer fields from the event.

documents.title: Runbook: refund procedure
documents.context: This Meridian runbook is for authorized support and billing staff. It describes internal controls that must not appear in customer replies. A refund changes settled financial records. One person prepares the case. Another authorized person approves values above the stated threshold. Never promise approval before review. Confirm the organization, invoice, payment, currency, and requestor authority. Record every decision in the billing case. Use only the payment console linked from the internal tools directory. Customer-facing guidance can explain timing and outcome after approval. It must not expose risk scores, reviewer notes, console identifiers, or internal escalation routes.
pages: Start a refund case only for a settled card charge or a confirmed overpayment. Link the organization and invoice in the case system. Confirm the request came from an owner or billing administrator through a verified support channel. Record one reason. Use duplicate charge, service outage credit, accidental renewal, tax correction, contract adjustment, or other. Add a short explanation. Check for earlier refunds and active disputes. A bank dispute takes priority because a separate refund can create a double credit. If a dispute exists, stop and route the case to Billing Risk. Calculate the refundable amount from settled line items, not from the customer's estimate. Keep tax in the same proportion as the refunded charge unless Finance has issued a correction instruction.

A refund up to 500 USD equivalent needs one Billing Specialist approval. A larger refund, any refund after ninety days, or any refund to a different payment route needs Billing Lead approval. Convert non-USD values with the settlement exchange amount shown in the console; do not use a current market rate. Attach the invoice, payment record, amount calculation, request evidence, and reason before requesting approval. The approver must not be the preparer. Approval expires after two business days if the payment state changes. Recheck for disputes immediately before execution. Contract credits are not card refunds and follow the account team's credit memo process. Partial refunds cannot exceed the remaining settled amount after earlier refunds, credits, or chargebacks.

After approval, open the payment through the case link and select Refund. Enter the approved amount and case identifier. The payment console displays the destination card and estimated processing window. Compare the last four digits with the original payment record; never ask the customer to provide a replacement card. Submit once and wait for the resulting refund identifier. A timeout can hide a successful submission, so refresh the payment record before trying again. Copy the refund identifier, amount, currency, destination, processor state, and execution time into the case. A pending refund normally reaches the issuer within five to ten business days. Meridian cannot accelerate the issuer's posting step. Keep the case open until the console shows accepted or failed.

Send the approved customer response from the case template. State the amount, currency, original invoice, execution date, and normal issuer window. Do not include the processor identifier, approval threshold, approver, risk review, or internal reason code. For a failed refund, do not retry until the failure reason is reviewed. An invalid destination routes to Billing Risk. A processor outage routes to the billing incident channel and remains pending. Close the case only after accepted status and a complete audit record. Add the refund to the weekly reconciliation queue. If the customer reports no credit after ten business days, confirm accepted status. Provide the customer-facing reference generated by the console. Escalate to Finance Operations with the case link; do not contact the processor directly.

documents.title: Runbook: billing escalation paths
documents.context: This internal Meridian runbook routes billing cases to the team that can act. It is not customer-facing policy. Support owns clear intake, identity verification, evidence collection, and status updates. Billing Operations owns invoice and payment corrections. Finance owns accounting treatment and reconciliation. Billing Risk owns disputes and suspicious payment changes. Account teams own contract interpretation. Do not send a case to several teams at once. Choose the primary path, state the requested decision, and add watchers only when another team supplies evidence. Keep customer promises limited to the published response time. Internal queue names, staffing schedules, risk signals, and approval notes must remain in the case system.
pages: Route an invoice address or legal-name correction to Billing Operations. Use this route when the invoice is unpaid and under thirty days old. Include organization, invoice number, requested text, current billing profile, and verified requestor role. Route completed invoice tax treatment to Finance Tax with the tax registration evidence already stored through the secure form. Do not accept tax documents by ordinary email. A request to change currency or billing interval follows Account Management when an Enterprise order form controls the subscription. Self-service customers can use portal settings for the next renewal. If the customer asks why a charge exists, support should first map it to plan, seats, prorated change, or renewal. Escalate only when the portal and payment record do not explain the amount.

Route card declines and retry timing to Billing Operations after the customer updates the payment method once. Support must not ask the issuer for details. Route duplicate settled charges to the refund procedure with both payment identifiers. Route an active chargeback, fraud claim, or request to refund another card to Billing Risk immediately. Stop any parallel refund. Add the exact customer statement without interpreting intent. Lock payment-setting changes only when Billing Risk directs it. A failed bank transfer with a trace document goes to Finance Receivables through secure attachment. Record amount, currency, send date, originating bank country, and invoice. Never copy bank account details into a general support comment. Use restricted case fields for financial identifiers.

Set severity by business impact, not customer tone. A single incorrect invoice with a workaround is normal priority. A payment failure that makes one organization read-only is high priority. A platform error charging several organizations or creating repeated invoices is incident priority and must page the Billing Incident Commander. Search active incidents before creating another. The escalation summary must state observed behavior, expected behavior, affected count, and first known time. It must also state the financial exposure estimate and completed containment. Use ranges when exact exposure is unknown and mark assumptions. Do not calculate public service credits during incident response. The incident commander coordinates any broad correction. Support continues verified customer updates from the approved incident message.

Billing Operations acknowledges normal cases within one business day and high-priority access cases within two hours during coverage. Incident priority uses the on-call page and requires acknowledgment within fifteen minutes. If an owner misses the target, escalate once to the queue lead with the case link and impact. Do not duplicate the case or contact individual engineers. Customer updates should state the next update time even when no decision exists. After resolution, confirm the payment or invoice state in the source system. Send the approved explanation and link any refund or credit record. Close child tasks before the support case. Add recurring causes to the monthly billing review with counts and examples stripped of customer data. A process gap belongs in that review, not in a customer-facing note.

documents.title: Runbook: verified account recovery
documents.context: This internal runbook covers a Meridian member who cannot use the normal password, authenticator, recovery-code, or identity-provider path. Recovery can expose organization data, so convenience never replaces verification. Support must not disable authentication from an unverified request. Keep all evidence in the restricted recovery case. Do not ask for passwords, authenticator codes, or full identity documents in normal email. Prefer restoration by an existing organization owner or identity-provider administrator. Manual recovery is the final path and requires two staff roles. Customer messages describe the next safe step without revealing which private signals passed or failed.
pages: First identify the sign-in mode from the organization security record. For SSO, ask the member to use the organization address. Route assignment or provider challenge issues to their identity administrator. Meridian must not bypass SSO. For local sign-in, confirm that the member tried a current password reset and automatic device time. Also confirm that the member tried a fresh authenticator code and any saved recovery code. Search for an active security incident or recent organization domain change. Record the member email, organization address, request time, last successful sign-in as stated by the member, and displayed request reference. Do not confirm whether an email belongs to an organization until the request channel has been verified.

The preferred recovery uses an active owner. Send the owner a secure approval request from the case system. The owner confirms the member, role, and need for restoration. Approval remains valid for four hours and applies only to the named member. If no active owner can respond, a Recovery Specialist checks the organization's verified domain control and billing-admin contact. Enterprise organizations can define a named security contact in their contract; use that path when present. Never accept a forwarded approval email, a screenshot of an inbox, or caller identification as sufficient evidence. Send requests involving the final owner, a recent domain change, or a disputed organization to Security Review. These requests cannot use the normal owner-assisted path.

After approval, a Recovery Specialist prepares a one-time recovery session. A second Support Lead checks the case evidence and authorizes release. The session link goes only to the verified member address through the case system. It expires after twenty minutes and works once. It requires a new password and new authenticator enrollment when organization policy requires them. Do not paste the link into chat or a case comment. The recovery action revokes all browser sessions and local recovery codes. It does not change API tokens, so an owner must review active tokens separately when compromise is suspected. Record preparer, approver, release time, recipient, expiration, and completion state. Never record the link value itself.

After recovery, tell the member to sign in from a trusted device. Tell them to generate new recovery codes and review active sessions. Notify the approving owner. Keep the case open for twenty-four hours when compromise was suspected. Route unexpected token use, changed billing settings, exported data, or unknown administrators to Security Incident Response. If verification fails, state that Meridian cannot change access through the current request. Name the available owner or contract process. Do not reveal the failed evidence or suggest how to imitate a valid signal. Close an expired unused session and require a new approval for another attempt. Monthly audit reviews every manual recovery for complete evidence, separate preparer and approver, correct delivery channel, and post-recovery notification.

documents.title: Runbook: temporary rate-limit overrides
documents.context: This internal runbook governs temporary Meridian API rate increases. Normal limits protect service stability and fair capacity. Support cannot grant an override in chat or edit a limit directly. An override needs a defined operation, measured request pattern, start and end time, rollback owner, and Capacity approval. It never changes storage, export, or scheduled-run quotas. Customer communication can state the approved temporary rate and expiration. It must not disclose global capacity, other organizations, alert thresholds, or internal dashboards. Prefer client pacing, caching, and batch endpoints before an override. Every increase expires automatically and must be reviewed after use.
pages: Collect the organization identifier, client name, endpoint set, current request rate, and required peak rate. Also collect expected duration, business reason, and planned concurrency. Ask for a recent 429 request identifier and the Retry-After value. Confirm the client already uses bounded retries with exponential backoff and random variation. Check whether batch endpoints or lower polling frequency meet the need. Reject requests framed as permanent headroom without measured usage. Search active incidents and the capacity calendar. Do not approve increases during a related service incident, maintenance window, or known saturation period. Support creates the request but does not choose a safe rate. Mark customer estimates clearly and avoid copying tokens, request bodies, or customer data into the capacity case.

A standard temporary override can double the normal per-organization request rate for up to six hours. It requires Capacity Engineer approval. A higher multiplier, longer period, write-heavy endpoint, or concurrent export launch also requires the Service Owner. Capacity reviews regional headroom, endpoint cost, current error budget, and monitoring coverage. The approver sets the exact rate, burst allowance, start, expiration, and abort thresholds. Approval is invalid if the requested window moves by more than one hour or the client pattern changes. Create a new review rather than editing an approved value. Never stack two overrides for the same organization. The control plane keeps the lower expiration when duplicate records exist.

Before activation, link the customer case, approval, organization, rate, burst, start, expiration, and rollback owner in the override tool. Read the confirmation back to the approver. Activate no earlier than fifteen minutes before the planned operation. Confirm the Usage page reflects a temporary limit and run one customer verification request. Watch gateway saturation, endpoint latency, 5xx rate, queue depth, and the organization's 429 rate for the first ten minutes. The customer must have an operator who can reduce traffic. If an abort threshold fires, disable the override and tell the customer to stop or pace work. Do not wait for additional approval to restore the normal safe limit. Record every activation, edit, and rollback time.

The override expires automatically at its recorded UTC time. Confirm normal limits after expiration and tell the customer before the end when work remains. Extensions require a new capacity review with actual request rate, errors, and remaining workload. After the window, record peak rate, total requests, 429 count, 5xx count, latency change, and whether abort thresholds fired. Close the request only after the control plane and Usage page show the normal limit. A successful override does not justify a permanent increase. Repeated need goes to Product Capacity Planning with measured data and an account-team owner. Remove customer identifiers from the monthly capacity summary. Any manual state that survives expiration is a control failure and must be reported to the Service Owner immediately.

documents.title: Incident review: delayed exports, April 2026
documents.context: This internal Meridian incident review records a resolved export delay from April 2026. It is operational history, not current customer guidance. The event affected asynchronous CSV and PDF creation while interactive dashboards remained available. Support may use the approved summary to recognize a similar symptom. Support must check current status before saying an incident exists. Internal queue sizes, deployment details, customer counts, and staff actions remain private. The purpose is to preserve detection, containment, recovery, and follow-up lessons. A matching symptom can have another cause. Responders must collect current export references and timing instead of assuming this event returned.
pages: The incident began at 09:12 UTC after an export-worker deployment increased memory used by wide table rendering. Workers restarted under load and returned unfinished jobs to the queue. The customer symptom was an export remaining Processing beyond fifteen minutes, followed by occasional Failed status. Dashboard queries and existing file downloads continued normally. The first alert came from queue age at 09:19. Support linked three high-priority cases by 09:27. The incident commander declared severity two at 09:31 because several organizations were affected without data loss. No completed file contained incorrect data. Scheduled deliveries were delayed with the same queue. API start requests continued to accept work, which increased backlog until containment.

Containment started at 09:38 by pausing new scheduled exports and reducing the maximum wide-table concurrency. The team rolled back the worker deployment at 09:44. Existing jobs were not deleted because each carried an idempotent job identifier and could resume safely. Support used the approved message that exports were delayed and dashboards remained available. Agents were told not to ask customers to create repeat jobs. At 09:52 queue age stopped increasing. Memory restarts ended after replacement workers became ready. The team sampled completed files from before and after rollback and found no content difference. New manual exports reopened gradually by region at 10:05. Scheduled work stayed paused until enough capacity existed for both old and new jobs.

Recovery was declared at 10:46 after queue age stayed below five minutes for twenty minutes. Paused schedules resumed in controlled groups. Jobs older than their source snapshot deadline failed with a clear retry message instead of producing stale files. Support received a query listing customer-visible failed references so agents could send targeted updates. The incident affected 184 export jobs across 37 fictional organizations. One hundred sixty-three completed after delay, and twenty-one required a customer restart. No daily export quota counted a Meridian-caused failed job. The status page closed at 11:03 after final verification. Case owners followed up with affected high-priority customers using the public resolution summary and no internal capacity figures.

The root cause was a layout-library option that retained large intermediate table structures across page batches. Review focused on output correctness but did not include a memory measurement for the widest supported table. Follow-up added a representative wide-table benchmark, a per-worker memory guard, and a staged concurrency check before full rollout. Queue acceptance now reduces automatically when restart rate crosses its threshold. The export service dashboard gained separate manual and scheduled queue age. Support training added the instruction to preserve one export reference and avoid duplicate starts during a broad delay. The deployment checklist now names memory, queue age, completion rate, and file sampling. These controls reduce recurrence but do not make every long Processing state an incident; agents still check current telemetry.

documents.title: Incident review: SSO redirect loop, June 2026
documents.context: This internal Meridian incident review records a resolved single sign-on redirect loop from June 2026. It helps responders distinguish platform symptoms from an individual identity-provider configuration error. It does not authorize support to bypass SSO or change a customer's provider. The public symptom was repeated movement between Meridian and the provider after successful authentication. Local-password organizations were unaffected. Internal deployment identifiers, affected counts, provider logs, and response coordination remain private. Agents must check current status and collect a request reference before associating a new case with an incident. A private browser test remains useful because stale cookies can create a similar loop for one member.
pages: The event began at 14:03 UTC after a gateway configuration release changed how encoded organization state was normalized. Some SSO organizations had uppercase characters in an older connection identifier. Their members returned to the organization selector without completing a session. The identity provider showed success, so administrators initially suspected assignment. A sign-in loop alert fired at 14:08 when repeated callback counts rose above baseline. Support linked the first two cases at 14:11 and included organization addresses and request references. The incident commander declared severity two at 14:16. Password sign-in, active sessions, API tokens, and SSO organizations with normalized identifiers continued working. No authentication assertion was accepted for the wrong organization.

The team stopped the gateway rollout at 14:20 and routed affected callbacks to the previous configuration at 14:24. Support published a message that some SSO sign-ins were looping and existing sessions remained valid. Agents asked affected members to keep sessions open and avoid repeated configuration edits. A private browser did not fix the incident cases, which separated them from stale local cookies. Identity administrators did not need to change assignments, certificates, or callback URLs. The gateway team compared callback traces using request references, never raw assertions. A safe normalization patch passed replay tests against older and current connection identifiers. It deployed to one region at 14:41 while the rollback continued serving other traffic.

Successful sign-in rate returned to normal in the canary region at 14:47. The patch expanded by region and completed at 15:02. Monitoring confirmed that callback counts fell and session creation matched successful provider responses. Support asked linked customers to start one new private browser session from the organization address. All confirmed recovery. The incident closed at 15:26 after twenty minutes of stable sign-in data. Forty-two fictional organizations had at least one failed callback and no account data changed. Repeated failed callbacks did not lock local profiles. The public resolution stated that Meridian corrected an SSO routing issue. It did not name identifier formats, gateway configuration, or affected organization counts. Case owners corrected any earlier advice that suggested provider changes.

The release test set covered current connection identifiers but not legacy mixed-case values that remained valid. The configuration compiler also normalized state differently from the callback service, which made review difficult. Follow-up created one canonical normalization function and fixtures for every supported identifier generation. Canary analysis now compares provider success with Meridian session creation rather than watching gateway errors alone. Support tools show a safe loop indicator from request references without exposing assertion content. The runbook adds one decision point. One user plus a successful private window suggests local cookies or assignment. Several users across organizations suggest current status review. This is diagnostic guidance, not proof. Responders still avoid provider edits during a broad platform incident unless evidence identifies a separate configuration fault.

documents.title: Runbook: security escalation
documents.context: This internal Meridian runbook helps support recognize and route a possible security event. Support does not investigate beyond approved evidence collection and immediate containment controls. Do not label a customer or member as malicious. Do not promise that no access occurred. Preserve timestamps, request references, organization identifiers, and the customer's exact observation. Keep secrets and sensitive evidence in the restricted security case. A suspected token exposure, unauthorized administrator, unexpected export, changed authentication setting, or cross-organization data view requires prompt review. Customer replies acknowledge concern and state completed safe actions. They give the next update time without disclosing detection rules or internal responders.
pages: Open a restricted security case for unrecognized access reported by a verified organization owner. Also open one when product telemetry links a security flag to a support request. Record reporter identity, organization, affected member or token prefix, first and last known times, observed action, and available request references. Copy the customer's wording and separate it from support assumptions. Do not request full tokens, passwords, authenticator codes, or unrestricted log archives. If a screenshot is necessary, provide the secure upload route and ask the customer to remove unrelated personal data. Search for an active platform incident that explains the symptom without closing the security path. Notify the Security Duty Officer through the case action, not by personal message.

Immediate containment must be reversible and proportional. A verified owner can revoke a named token or sign out member sessions. The owner can also suspend a member or disable a webhook through normal controls. Support can guide those actions. Support must not delete audit history, remove data, or change an identity-provider configuration. The Security Duty Officer can authorize a temporary organization security hold. Use it when current access causes harm and the owner cannot act. Record exact scope, start time, approver, customer impact, and review time. A hold can block sign-in or writes while preserving evidence. Do not announce a broad breach from one signal. Tell the customer which access was revoked or paused and when the next status update will arrive.

Security triage classifies credential exposure, account takeover, data access, data change, integration abuse, or suspected cross-tenant access. Cross-tenant evidence pages the incident commander immediately, even if only one request is known. The duty officer correlates audit events, gateway records, token use, exports, and configuration changes. Support continues collecting customer-visible facts and avoids independent searches in production data. Preserve original time zones and add UTC equivalents. Do not paste raw log lines into general case comments. If law enforcement, regulatory notice, or legal preservation is mentioned, add Legal through the restricted workflow. Account teams can observe customer impact but do not direct technical containment. Every external statement comes from the incident communications owner after review.

Close support ownership only after Security records the classification, containment state, customer communication owner, and next action. A false positive still needs a concise reason and preserved evidence. A confirmed event moves to the security incident process and can remain open beyond the support case. Tell the customer how to complete any required password, authenticator, token, member, or webhook rotation. Do not provide internal root-cause detail before approval. After resolution, confirm temporary holds were removed and normal organization access works. The review checks response time, evidence quality, containment authority, customer updates, and any unsafe data shared during intake. Repeated confusion in product messages becomes a security usability issue. Add it to the improvement queue without copying customer identifiers or restricted evidence.

documents.title: Runbook: data deletion requests
documents.context: This internal Meridian runbook routes organization data deletion requests. Deletion can be irreversible and may conflict with billing, legal, or security retention. Support never starts deletion from an unverified chat request. An organization owner submits the product request, and Privacy Operations confirms scope and authority. The process distinguishes deleting one source, one member profile, one workspace, or the whole organization. Normal product controls should handle ordinary content removal. This runbook covers requests that need backend erasure or a formal privacy record. Customer messages state scope and timing without listing internal storage systems, backup design, legal review notes, or staff assignments.
pages: Identify the requested subject and desired result. Ask whether the request covers an imported data source, dashboard, workspace, member profile, billing record, support case, or entire organization. Explain that deleting a dashboard does not delete its source and removing a member does not erase audit history. Verify the requestor as an active owner through the signed-in support channel. A former member requesting personal profile deletion follows the privacy identity process rather than owner verification. Record the organization, scope, business reason if offered, applicable deadline stated by the customer, and any active contract closure. Do not ask the customer to include personal data examples unless scope cannot otherwise be identified. Use restricted fields for subject identifiers.

Check holds before approval. An active payment dispute can retain transaction evidence. A security incident can preserve relevant audit and access records. Legal can impose a preservation hold. Enterprise contracts can define return or deletion steps at termination. Privacy Operations decides how these obligations affect scope and timing. Support does not interpret law or promise a date before that review. Product content without a hold can usually enter deletion promptly. Backups age out under the retention schedule and are not selectively edited. Customer-facing wording can state the approved backup retention window but must not describe infrastructure locations. If part of the request cannot be erased, the decision owner supplies the category, basis, access restriction, and approved explanation.

For approved backend deletion, Privacy Operations creates a job with the organization and scoped resource identifiers. The job also contains the approval record, hold check, and completion deadline. A separate operator reviews the scope before execution. The deletion tool first produces a dry-run count by data category. Compare that count with the case and stop on an unexpected organization or resource. Execute once using the case identifier. Record the job identifier, operator, reviewer, start, result counts, and any retained categories. A timeout requires checking job state before another attempt. Deletion jobs are idempotent, but duplicate execution complicates audit evidence. Product access can be suspended during whole-organization deletion. Do not tell a customer that deletion is complete while any required production category remains pending.

Privacy Operations verifies completion from job results and approved sampling. Support then sends the customer-facing confirmation with request scope, completion date, and any disclosed retention exception. Do not include table names, storage locations, internal job identifiers, or reviewer names. Close the support case only after the privacy record holds the verification. If a job partially fails, keep access restrictions in place and route the failed category to its system owner. Give the customer a new update time, not an estimated success claim. Monthly review checks overdue requests, repeated partial failures, incorrect scope, and missing verification. Product gaps that force manual deletion become privacy engineering work. Use fictional or redacted examples in improvement tickets and never copy actual customer data.

documents.title: Runbook: enterprise entitlement repair
documents.context: This internal Meridian runbook handles an Enterprise organization whose signed features or seat quantity do not match product entitlements. The contract and approved order record are authoritative. Support can diagnose and collect evidence, but only Billing Operations or Account Provisioning can change entitlements. Do not use an override to settle a contract disagreement. Temporary repair prevents business interruption while the account team confirms ambiguous terms. Customer communication names restored features and duration without exposing provisioning systems, internal product codes, pricing, or approval discussion. Every manual repair needs an owner, expiration, and reconciliation task so temporary state cannot become an undocumented permanent contract.
pages: Confirm the organization, affected feature, observed message, first known time, and business impact. Check the Billing plan view, entitlement audit, latest active order record, and scheduled renewal change. A feature can disappear after an order ends, a renewal amendment starts, or a provisioning event fails. It can also disappear when the organization address points to another tenant. Do not assume a billing problem from a user role restriction. Test with the owner's permission view and identify whether the feature is absent for all authorized members. Record safe screenshots or error references. Search active provisioning incidents. Link the account owner and contract record in the restricted case. Do not copy prices, discounts, or contract attachments into general support comments.

Route a missing feature to Account Provisioning when the active order clearly grants it. Use this route when the audit shows a failed or missing provisioning event. Include organization identifier, order identifier, product code from the order, expected start and end, observed entitlement, and event status. A provisioning specialist replays the approved event or corrects mapping. When the order is unclear, expired, unsigned, or conflicts with another amendment, route to the account owner. Do not change product state until Commercial Operations resolves the contract. A seat shortage caused by active members is not entitlement failure; use the seat process. A feature blocked by workspace role is access configuration. Keep those paths separate so repair does not broaden access unnecessarily.

A verified active order must support the feature before approval of a temporary entitlement. Repair must also exceed the high-priority response target. Account Provisioning Lead approves up to twenty-four hours. Longer access also needs the account owner and Commercial Operations. Enter the exact feature, organization, seat cap if relevant, start, expiration, reason, and rollback owner. Never grant a bundle when one feature is affected. Confirm the product displays the temporary expiration and tell the customer that service is restored while records are reconciled. Monitor entitlement changes during the window. A permanent provisioning event should replace the temporary record before expiration. Two temporary records for one feature are prohibited because their rollback order is ambiguous.

After permanent repair, compare product entitlements with the active order line by line. Remove the temporary record and verify that access remains. Ask the customer to retry the affected workflow. Record repair event, verification time, temporary removal, customer confirmation, and any usage created during temporary access. If contract review denies the feature, the account owner leads communication before temporary expiration. Support does not describe that outcome as a technical failure. Close the incident only after the audit shows one supported source for each entitlement and no manual record without expiration. Monthly reconciliation lists all temporary grants, owners, expirations, and permanent outcomes. A repeated mapping fault becomes provisioning engineering work with contract values removed from the technical example.

documents.title: Runbook: webhook delivery triage
documents.context: This internal Meridian runbook helps support triage webhook delivery failures without receiving customer secrets or payload data. Public guidance covers endpoint setup, signature verification, retries, and history. Internal tools can inspect delivery metadata, gateway outcome, and retry schedule. They do not display the signing secret. Support should separate one endpoint configuration problem from a broad delivery incident. Never replay many events as a diagnostic action. A replay can trigger customer automation and must be approved by the endpoint owner. Customer replies can name delivery status, attempt time, response status, and next safe action. They must not name internal queue topology or detection thresholds.
pages: Collect organization address, endpoint identifier, event type, and event identifier when known. Also collect delivery identifier, UTC attempt time, displayed status, and receiver response code. Ask whether all events fail or only one event type. Confirm the endpoint is enabled and recent history exists. Do not ask for the signing secret, Authorization values returned by the receiver, or a full event payload. If the customer supplies a payload, move it to the approved secure route and remove it from ordinary comments. Check current webhook status and failure rate across organizations. One endpoint with DNS, TLS, timeout, 401, or 4xx responses usually indicates receiver configuration. Several unrelated endpoints with gateway errors can indicate a Meridian incident.

Use delivery metadata to follow the path. No route means event selection did not include that type or the endpoint was disabled when the event occurred. Queued means the event awaits delivery capacity. Attempting means a worker owns it. Retry scheduled means the last attempt timed out or returned a retryable response. Delivered means a 2xx response was accepted. Disabled by 410 means the receiver explicitly removed the endpoint. Signature rejected appears to Meridian only as the receiver's 401 or 403; support cannot verify customer code. Compare attempt duration with the five-second deadline. For DNS, certificate, connection, or timeout failures, give the public network checklist. Do not reveal resolved internal addresses or infrastructure regions.

A manual replay needs a verified endpoint owner and a statement that repeat processing is safe. Replay one event first. Record approver, event identifier, reason, and replay delivery identifier. The replay uses the current endpoint configuration and signing secret, not the configuration from the original attempt. A delivered replay proves current reachability but does not prove the original event was processed. Ask the customer to confirm its stable event identifier in receiver records. Do not replay a bulk range from support tools. A large missed interval routes to Integration Operations, which can assess capacity and customer idempotency. If Meridian caused the failure, preserve quota and retry behavior from the incident plan. Do not ask every customer to start replays.

Declare a webhook incident when several organizations show a common Meridian transport failure. Also declare one when queue age passes the alert threshold with customer impact. Link representative deliveries from different organizations and page the Integration Incident Commander. Avoid testing customer endpoints during containment. Support uses the approved incident message and provides the next update time. After recovery, the service drains retryable deliveries within their twenty-four-hour window. Expired events require a reviewed recovery plan because automatic bulk replay can duplicate business actions. Close an individual case after current delivery succeeds or you identify the receiver issue. Document who owns the next action. The weekly review tracks failure categories, long receiver times, repeated 410 disablement, and replay use. It also tracks cases where sensitive payload content entered an unsafe channel.
